learn: Scientists ask a question, research, form a testable hypothesis, experiment, analyse data and draw conclusions.
A hypothesis is often written "If..., then... because..."
Results are shared so others can repeat and check them.
check: Scientists share results so others can...
lessons.try: Write a hypothesis for whether plants grow faster with music.

learn: The independent variable is what you change; the dependent variable is what you measure.
Controlled variables are kept the same to make a fair test.
A control group gets no treatment for comparison.
check: What you change is the ___ variable.
What you measure is the ___ variable.
Keeping other factors the same makes a...
lessons.try: Identify the variables in an experiment on ball bounce height.

learn: Scientists use SI (metric) units: metres, kilograms, seconds, kelvins, litres.
Prefixes: kilo- (1,000), centi- (1/100), milli- (1/1,000).
Repeat trials and average them to reduce error.
check: The SI unit of mass is the...
lessons.try: Measure an object three times and calculate the average.

learn: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space.
Physical properties can be observed without changing the substance: colour, density, melting point, conductivity.
Density = mass ÷ volume. Objects less dense than water float.
check: An object less dense than water will...
lessons.try: Calculate the density of a block of wood from its mass and volume.

learn: In solids, particles vibrate in fixed positions. In liquids they slide past each other. In gases they move freely and spread out.
Adding thermal energy speeds particles up.
Plasma, found in stars and lightning, is a fourth state.
check: Particles move most freely in a...
lessons.try: Draw particle diagrams for a solid, a liquid and a gas.

learn: Melting: solid to liquid. Freezing: liquid to solid. Evaporation: liquid to gas. Condensation: gas to liquid.
Sublimation goes directly from solid to gas, as dry ice does.
Temperature stays constant during a change of state while energy breaks or forms bonds.
lessons.try: Watch ice melt and record the temperature every minute.

learn: Atoms contain protons (positive) and neutrons (neutral) in the nucleus, with electrons (negative) around it.
The number of protons is the atomic number and defines the element.
In a neutral atom, electrons equal protons.
check: The atomic number is the number of...
lessons.try: Draw a model of a carbon atom (6 protons, 6 neutrons, 6 electrons).

learn: Dmitri Mendeleev organised the elements into a table in 1869.
Rows are periods; columns are groups. Elements in a group have similar properties.
Metals are on the left, nonmetals on the right and metalloids in between.
check: Who organised the first periodic table?
Columns in the periodic table are...
lessons.try: Find the symbols for ten common elements.

learn: An element is made of one kind of atom. A compound is two or more elements chemically joined, like water (H₂O).
A mixture combines substances without chemical bonding, like sand and salt.
Mixtures can be separated by physical means: filtering, evaporating, magnets.
check: Sand and salt together is a...
lessons.try: Sort ten substances into elements, compounds and mixtures.

learn: A physical change alters form but not the substance: cutting paper, melting ice.
A chemical change creates new substances: rusting, cooking an egg, digesting food.
Signs of a chemical change: colour change, gas bubbles, light or temperature change, a new solid forming.
check: Gas bubbles can be a sign of a...
lessons.try: Sort ten everyday changes into physical and chemical.

learn: In a chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed.
The total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products.
Antoine Lavoisier demonstrated this in the 1700s.
check: Mass of reactants equals mass of...
Conservation of mass was shown by...
lessons.try: Watch a video of a reaction in a sealed bag on a balance and note the mass.

learn: Photosynthesis, respiration, digestion and rusting are all chemical reactions.
Reactions either release energy (exothermic, like a hand warmer) or absorb it (endothermic, like an instant cold pack).
Only carry out reactions in class with a teacher and proper safety equipment.
check: A reaction that releases heat is...
Reactions in school should be done...
With a teacher and safety gear
lessons.try: List five chemical reactions that happen in your home.

learn: A force is a push or pull, measured in newtons (N).
Balanced forces cause no change in motion; unbalanced forces cause acceleration.
Friction opposes motion; gravity pulls objects together.
lessons.try: Draw force arrows on a book resting on a table and a box being pushed.

learn: First law (inertia): an object stays at rest or in steady motion unless an unbalanced force acts.
Second law: force = mass × acceleration (F = ma).
A heavier object needs more force for the same acceleration.
check: Inertia is described by Newton's ___ law.
A 2 kg object accelerating at 3 m/s² needs ___ N.
lessons.try: Push an empty and a full trolley and compare.

learn: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.
A swimmer pushes water back; the water pushes the swimmer forward.
Rockets push gas out; the gas pushes the rocket up.
check: A swimmer moves forward because water pushes...
A balloon flies because air pushes...
Out one way, balloon goes the other
lessons.try: Release a blown-up balloon and explain its motion.

learn: Speed = distance ÷ time.
A car travelling 150 km in 3 hours averages 50 km/h.
Distance-time graphs show speed as slope.
check: On a distance-time graph, speed is the...
lessons.try: Time yourself walking 20 metres and calculate your speed.

learn: Velocity is speed in a given direction: 20 m/s north.
Two cars at the same speed but going opposite ways have different velocities.
Velocity changes if speed or direction changes.
lessons.try: Describe the velocity of a ball thrown upward at three moments.

learn: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: (final - initial) ÷ time.
A bike going from 0 to 10 m/s in 5 s accelerates at 2 m/s².
Slowing down is negative acceleration (deceleration).
check: 0 to 10 m/s in 5 s is ___ m/s².
Acceleration is the change in ___ over time.
lessons.try: Roll a ball down a ramp and describe its acceleration.

learn: Kinetic energy is energy of motion; it increases with mass and speed.
Potential energy is stored energy, such as an object raised high (gravitational) or a stretched spring (elastic).
Energy is measured in joules (J).
check: A book on a high shelf has ___ energy.
lessons.try: Drop a ball from different heights and observe the bounce.

learn: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed.
On a roller coaster, potential energy at the top becomes kinetic energy at the bottom.
Some energy always becomes thermal energy due to friction.
check: At the bottom of a roller coaster, energy is mostly...
lessons.try: Trace energy changes when you ride a bike down a hill.

learn: Thermal energy moves from hot to cold.
Conduction: through direct contact. Convection: by moving fluids. Radiation: by electromagnetic waves.
Insulators slow heat transfer; conductors speed it up.
lessons.try: Test which cup material keeps water warm longest.

learn: Waves transfer energy without transferring matter.
Wavelength is the distance between crests; frequency is waves per second (hertz); amplitude is height.
Mechanical waves need a medium; electromagnetic waves do not.
lessons.try: Make waves in a rope or slinky and change the frequency.

learn: Sound is a mechanical wave that travels through solids, liquids and gases, but not a vacuum.
Higher frequency means higher pitch; larger amplitude means louder.
Sound travels about 343 m/s in air.
check: Sound travels in air at about...
lessons.try: Estimate the distance to lightning by counting seconds before thunder.

learn: Light is an electromagnetic wave that travels at about 300,000 km/s.
The spectrum includes radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.
Light reflects, refracts (bends) and is absorbed.
lessons.try: Use a glass of water to see refraction bend a pencil.

learn: Electric charges can be positive or negative; like charges repel, opposites attract.
Current is the flow of charge, measured in amperes.
Conductors (metals) let current flow; insulators (rubber, plastic) don't.
lessons.try: Rub a balloon on your hair and observe static electricity.

learn: A circuit needs a power source, wires and a load (like a bulb), in a complete loop.
Series circuits have one path; if one bulb goes out, all go out.
Parallel circuits have several paths, as in home wiring.
check: In a series circuit, if one bulb fails...
lessons.try: Use a circuit simulator to build series and parallel circuits.

learn: Magnets have north and south poles; like poles repel.
Electric current creates a magnetic field: electromagnets.
Moving a magnet near a coil generates current: this is how generators work.
check: Current in a coil creates a...
lessons.try: Make an electromagnet with a battery, a wire and an iron nail (with a teacher).

learn: Gravity is a force that acts at a distance through a field.
Its strength depends on mass and distance.
Weight is the force of gravity on mass: on the Moon you weigh about one-sixth as much.
check: On the Moon you weigh about...
lessons.try: Calculate your weight on the Moon.

learn: Fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) are nonrenewable and release carbon dioxide when burned.
Renewable resources include solar, wind, hydroelectric and geothermal energy.
Nuclear power produces little carbon dioxide but creates radioactive waste.
lessons.try: Make a chart of the pros and cons of five energy sources.

learn: Engineers design solutions to energy problems: better batteries, efficient homes, electric vehicles.
The engineering design process: define, research, brainstorm, build, test, improve.
Every solution has trade-offs in cost, efficiency and environmental impact.
lessons.try: Design a model house that keeps heat in.
